summary: This RFC extends the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for stateful PCE so that vendor-specific information can be carried in its messages. Vendors can include proprietary data to support their own optimizations, in a defined way that other implementations can recognize and safely ignore.

eli5.summary: A postal form with a box for notes lets a company add its own special details. Others can skip the box if they do not understand it.

questions: how to carry vendor-specific information in pcep
what is the pcep vendor information object
can pcep carry vendor specific data
how does pcep handle unknown enterprise numbers
subtitle: Lets stateful PCEP messages carry vendor-specific data, the same way RFC 7470 already did for stateless PCEP.

tldr.problem: RFC 7470 lets vendors carry proprietary information in stateless PCEP, but the stateful PCEP messages (PCRpt, PCUpd, PCInitiate) had no place for a Vendor Information object.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds an optional list of VENDOR-INFORMATION objects to the PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate messages, and confirms that the VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV can ride inside stateful objects. Receivers that do not know the Enterprise Number ignore the object.
tldr.outcome: Vendors can attach private data to stateful PCE exchanges without breaking legacy peers. It also updates RFC 7470 so that Enterprise Numbers point to the Private Enterprise Numbers registry.

today: RFC 9752 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025. It updates RFC 7470 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) ask a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute paths. A stateful PCE also knows about active paths and their reserved resources, which RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 support with extra messages.

RFC 7470 defined the Vendor Information object, which can carry arbitrary proprietary information such as vendor-specific constraints, but only for stateless PCEP. It also defined the VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV, which can be embedded in any PCEP object that supports TLVs. This document extends the object to the stateful messages.
sections.eli5: There was already a way to attach a private note to some network messages. This RFC lets the same kind of note be attached to the other kinds of messages too.

sections.title: Vendor Information in Stateful Messages
sections.content:
A PCC that wants to convey vendor-specific information to a PCE includes a Vendor Information object in the PCRpt message, which reports the current state of an LSP. A PCE can include it in a PCUpd message (which updates LSP attributes) and in a PCInitiate message (which triggers LSP instantiation or deletion). The object is OPTIONAL, and multiple instances MAY appear in one message, even with different Enterprise Numbers.

In each message the RBNF gains an optional <vendor-info-list>, which is one or more VENDOR-INFORMATION objects. In PCRpt and PCUpd it follows the <path>. In a PCInitiate instantiation it follows the optional <attribute-list>. The RBNF is only illustrative: if it disagrees with the descriptive text, the text wins.
sections.eli5: Three kinds of messages now each get an optional box at the end where a company can put its own notes.

sections.title: How Receivers Treat the Data
sections.content:
The receiver decides how to interpret the data by looking at the Enterprise Number inside the object. A legacy implementation that does not recognize the Vendor Information object follows the procedures of RFC 8231 and RFC 8281. An implementation that supports the object but sees an Enterprise Number it does not support MUST ignore the object, as described in Section 2 of RFC 7470.

The VENDOR-INFORMATION-TLV can also be placed inside a specific PCEP object, including stateful ones such as the SRP and LSP objects. All procedures for the TLV are those of Section 3 of RFC 7470.
sections.eli5: If you do not recognize the company that wrote the note, you simply skip it and carry on.

sections.title: The Update to RFC 7470
sections.content: RFC 7470 said Enterprise Numbers are assigned by IANA and managed through an IANA registry. This document replaces that text: Enterprise Numbers are assigned by IANA and managed through the "Private Enterprise Numbers (PENs)" registry as described in RFC 9371. That is the reason the RFC is marked as updating RFC 7470.
sections.eli5: The RFC fixes one sentence so it points to the right list of company numbers.

sections.title: Manageability and Network Impact
sections.content:
All manageability considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 7470, RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 apply. A standard YANG module will not include details of vendor-specific information, but it could be extended to report use of the object or TLV and the Enterprise Numbers they contain.

Extra vendor data may congest operations, as noted in Section 6.6 of RFC 7470. A PCEP speaker SHOULD NOT include vendor information in a stateful PCEP message if it believes the recipient does not support it. Encoding optimizations, such as when the same content is encoded for many LSPs, are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Do not send notes to someone who cannot read them, because that only clutters the mailbox.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions do not change the nature of PCEP, so the security considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 7470, RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 apply unchanged. Per RFC 8231, it is RECOMMENDED to activate these extensions only on authenticated and encrypted sessions using TLS (RFC 8253), following the best practices in RFC 9325.

Vendor-specific information may provide a covert channel that could be misused by implementations or by malicious software at PCEP speakers. Operators can monitor PCEP sessions to detect its use and inspect it, and should prevent installation of malicious software with robust integrity, authentication and authorization techniques, which are out of scope here.
sections.eli5: Private notes could be used to sneak secrets through, so people running the network should keep an eye on them.
